# Oblada

> Now in beta: a Chromium web browser with Zen's sidebar, Firefox's containers, Brave's protection from trackers, and add-ons from both the Chrome Web Store and Firefox Add-ons.

Oblada is a web browser with Zen's sidebar, Firefox's containers, Brave's protection from trackers, and add-ons from both the Chrome and Firefox stores. Built on Chromium, named after a fish. Oblada is in beta: free, open source, and for now on Macs with Apple Silicon. Linux builds are coming soon, then Windows.

- Latest version: 0.5.1, released 2026-10-28, based on Chromium 156.0.8078.48
- Download for Mac (Apple Silicon): https://github.com/Oblada-Browser/oblada/releases/latest/download/Oblada-silicon.dmg
- Source code (GPL-3.0): https://github.com/Oblada-Browser/oblada

## Features

- **Tabs down the side.** Vertical tabs in a sidebar, with room for long titles and dozens of tabs. The page gets the rest of the window.
- **Workspaces you swipe between.** Keep home, work and the weekend apart, and swipe with two fingers to move between them. Each workspace takes its own color, and can open its new tabs in a container of its own.
- **Two pages, one window.** Drag a tab onto the page to split the view. Drag the handle to swap sides, or onto the sidebar to separate them again.
- **An address bar that floats.** Press ⌘L and the address bar rises over the page like a buoy, with its suggestions right under it. Pick one and it drifts back to the sidebar.
- **Compact mode.** Hide the sidebar and the page gets the whole window. Reach for the left edge and the sidebar slides back in.
- **Window layouts.** Tabs down the side or along the top, the address bar wherever suits you: Oblada has seven window layouts. Pick one the first time you open it, and change it whenever you like, from the menu's Window layout or Settings › Oblada.
  - Sidebar (tabs on the side): Tabs, address bar and workspaces on the side
  - Scaffold (tabs on the side): Tabs as icons, the address bar on top
  - Expanded scaffold (tabs on the side): The full sidebar, the address bar on top
  - Compact (tabs on the side): Only the page: the sidebar shows from the left edge
  - Horizon (tabs at the top): The address bar on top, the tabs below it
  - Horizon compact (tabs at the top): One row: the active tab is the address bar
  - Classic (tabs at the top): The tabs on top, the address bar below them
- **Containers.** Each container keeps its own cookies, logins and site data. Open the same site in two containers and use two accounts side by side, with nothing seeping from one to the other. Eight colors, the same as Firefox's.
- **Temporary containers.** For one-off visits. Nothing is written to disk, and when the last tab closes the container pops, data and all.
- **Add-ons from two seas.** Install from the Chrome Web Store as usual, or straight from Firefox Add-ons: Oblada converts the .xpi while it installs. Firefox's contextualIdentities API comes along too, so add-ons like Multi-Account Containers work with Oblada's containers.
- **Protection from trackers.** The Barrier brings Brave's Shields to Oblada, on by default: it blocks trackers and ads, shows every site a slightly different you, and forgets what third parties leave behind.
  - **Trackers and ads, blocked.** With Brave's engine and the lists it uses: EasyList, EasyPrivacy, uBlock Origin's and Brave's own. The empty boxes they leave behind, cookie notices and anti-adblock walls go too.
  - **Third parties forget.** Their cookies are blocked, and what they store on a site is erased once you close it. Any site can be forgotten when you close it, too.
  - **Site by site.** Turn the Barrier off where a site breaks, block harder where it doesn't, block scripts: right from the address bar.
  - **A different you on every site.** Sites that fingerprint you read your canvas, audio, fonts, screen and processor. The Barrier changes them slightly: the same on a site until Oblada restarts, different on every other site and in every container.
  - **Links without the hooks.** Sites hang parameters on links to know who followed them. Oblada cuts them off the addresses you open, and skips tracking redirects and AMP pages for the real page.
  - And also: Global Privacy Control; HTTPS wherever it works; Trackers hiding behind a site's own addresses; Sensitive sites in a temporary container; A question before Google sign-in on other sites; Block any element; Your own filters and lists; Web APIs that mostly track you, off; A red switch that turns it all off.

Oblada's sidebar, workspaces, compact mode and split view follow the design of Zen Browser, an open-source browser built on Firefox by a small team. If you like how Oblada feels, thank the people who thought of it first.

The Barrier stands on Brave’s work: its adblock-rust engine, its lists, and its way of blurring fingerprints. Thank you, Brave.

## Installing

Oblada isn't signed by a registered Apple developer or notarized yet. It will be soon: until then, macOS stops it the first time you open it. To let it through:

1. Open the .dmg and drag Oblada to Applications.
2. Open Oblada, and close the warning macOS shows you.
3. Go to System Settings › Privacy & Security, scroll down and click Open Anyway.

If macOS says the app is damaged, run this in Terminal instead:

```sh
xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/Oblada.app
```

## What's new in 0.5.1

### Added

- Settings > Oblada > Privacy can turn off each protection Oblada applies as it starts: HTTPS memory (HSTS) and connections kept apart for each site, web features that mostly serve to recognize you, shorter referrers, cookies kept 6 months at most.

### Changed

- Firefox add-ons install and update only from addons.mozilla.org.
- Certificate Transparency is on, as in Chrome: sites' certificates must be in public logs.
- Sites' wish to always be opened over HTTPS (HSTS) is kept apart for each site when it comes from inside another site's pages, as in Brave, rather than holding for pages only.

### Fixed

- Safe Browsing works: Oblada warns before opening sites Google lists as phishing or malware, and before downloading files from addresses on its lists. Settings showed it on, but without a key for Google's Safe Browsing API it never got its lists.
- Security: another site could offer a Firefox add-on, or change where an installed one took its updates from, even if you said no.
- Security: a page sending a tab to a container, AMP pages left for the original and peeks opened sites as if you had typed their address, so other sites could act on them as you.
- Security: pages in containers could be prerendered, and searches prefetched, outside the container.
- Security: only uBlock Origin's and Brave's own filter lists can run their most powerful scripts, lists come over HTTPS only, and their rules can't have pages report where you are.
- Security: the Barrier checks where redirects lead, its questions (sensitive sites, Google sign-ins, blocked sites) can't be answered by the sites themselves, and only the page you picked an element on can add a filter.
